in.mechanism: The Fed's balance sheet is the numerator of net liquidity: what it buys, it pays for with money that did not exist before.
Cash parked overnight at the Fed is cash not in the market. Reverse repo draining is liquidity being released without the Fed buying anything.
Money in the Treasury's account has left the banking system. A tax date or a heavy auction fills it; government spending empties it back out.

out.breaks: Fails completely when the reason liquidity is rising is that something broke — 2008 and March 2020 both saw liquidity surge into falling equities.
out.mechanism: More money loose in the system has to go somewhere, and the deepest market is where it goes first.

out.breaks: Crypto-native shocks — an exchange failure, a forced liquidation cascade — swamp the liquidity signal for weeks at a time.
out.mechanism: Bitcoin has no earnings to fall back on, so its price is close to a pure function of how much spare money exists.

node.label: Net liquidity
node.up: There is more money loose in the system looking for somewhere to go
node.what: The Fed's balance sheet minus the two places money hides: reverse repo and the Treasury's cash account. It is the closest single number to 'how much money is actually circulating', and it is the tide that lifts and drops risk assets without anybody announcing anything.
